newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan moves to fight off U.S. shipping sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Japan moves to fight off U.S. shipping sanctions.

text.p: Japan is making last-ditch efforts to avert possible U.S. sanctions on Japanese shipping firms for what Washington says are unfair practices at Japanese ports, a Foreign Ministry official said on Wednesday.

The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC), is likely to come up with a decision on whether to impose sanctions in the next three weeks, the official said. The deadline for public comments to the commission passed on Tuesday.
"We want to avoid sanctions, considering the impact not only on shipping firms and cargo owners such as car makers, but also on Japan-U.S. relations," the official said.
U.S. and Japanese authorities were unable to narrow their differences at a meeting in Washington on January six and 7.
Last October, the European Union called for consultations with Japan under World Trade Organisation rules to make Japanese ports more accessible to foreign shippers.

The FMC is considering slapping a surcharge of $100,000 each time a ship owned by Japanese ship operators Mitsui O.S.K. Lines Ltd, Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd and Nippon Yusen KK stops at a U.S. port. The three leading shipping firms have regular routes to the United States.
The three firms on Tuesday sent their comments to the FMC, making clear their opposition to the proposed sanctions, a spokesman for Nippon Yusen KK said.
"The sanctions would cost the three firms an estimated combined five billion yen ($42.3 million) annually," he said.

The U.S. complaints are based on two main points, the need to consult with the Japan Harbour Transportation Association (JHTA) in advance on even minor changes to schedules, and restrictions laid down by the Transport Ministry in entering the loading and unloading business at Japanese ports.
The Japan Harbor Transportation Association, made up of port cargo-handling firms, is in charge of assigning loading, unloading and other work related to ships arriving at ports.
As a result, there is little competition among companies providing harbour services, and inefficient port operations have pushed Japanese port costs well above international levels.

To try to resolve the issues, the Transport Ministry is setting up a meeting between shipping firms -- both Japanese and foreign -- stevedore labour unions and the JHTA to try reach an agreement, the Foreign Ministry official said.
The meeting is expected to be held by the end of January.

The Transport Ministry also plans to ease restrictions on entering business at Japanese ports within three to five years, the official said. He said newcomers have been restricted in the past 10 years because of a surplus of stevedores.
Japan's harbour practices have long been a mystery to foreign shipowners and Japanese film makers have portrayed harbours as being controlled by the "Yakuza" or mafia.
